newsitem.title: USA: Ralston is joint chiefs candidate despite affair.
newsitem.headline: Ralston is joint chiefs candidate despite affair.

text.p: The White House and Pentagon said on Thursday that Air Force Gen. Joseph Ralston remained a leading candidate to become chairman of the military Joint Chiefs of Staff despite an adulterous affair 13 years ago.

That defiant decision not to scrap Ralston's candidacy for the nation's top military job was announced after he revealed the affair this week amid a major debate in Washington over marital morals and sexual harassment in the armed forces.

Ralston, vice chairman of the joint chiefs, took "full responsibility for my conduct some years ago" in a statement on Thursday thanking Defence Secretary William Cohen for confidence in "my ability to further serve this nation."
Ralston, 53, who was travelling in former Soviet states in Asia, gave no indication he will withdraw as a possible candidate to succeed Army Gen. John Shalikashvili this year.
Cohen said in a strong statement that Ralston was still among the top candidates he was considering and he would make a recommendation to President Bill Clinton within two weeks.

"General Ralston was a leading candidate before I learned of these events in his past and he is still a leading candidate. If I recommend General Ralston to the president I will do so in full confidence of his character and leadership," Cohen said.

Ralston this week disclosed to Cohen in response to media inquiries that he had had an affair with a civilian woman while he was a colonel and separated from his first wife 13 years ago. They were later reconciled but divorced in 1988.

The news followed a recent series of embarrassing cases in which U.S. military officers have been removed from command or retired over allegations of adultery or sexual harassment, both of which are strictly prohibited in the armed forces.
"The president has confidence in Cohen's judgment and in his thinking and will receive his recommendation and then make his decision," White House spokeswoman Anne Luzzatto said.

Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said the Ralston case was far different from that of the Air Force's first woman bomber pilot, Lt. Kelly Flinn, who was forced to resign last month to avoid a court martial on adultery and other charges.

But two Democratic congesswomen from New York said the Pentagon should review its sexual conduct policies in light of Ralston's possible promotion and Flinn's general discharge. "It is very clear that the Pentagn is selectively enforcing its rules on sexual conduct," Representative Nita Lowey said.
Representative Carolyn Maloney said: "If you are a friend of the secretary of defence and you've had an affair, you're in. If you are a successful woman who's had an affair you're out."

While adultery is a crime in the military, the Pentagon rarely prosecutes soldiers and officers for adultery. But service members have often been forced into early retirement or had their pay and rank reduced.

Defence officials say Ralston has been Cohen's favourite to succeed Shalikashvili but Marine Corps Gen. John Sheehan, head of the U.S. military's Atlantic Command in Norfolk, Virginia, is also high on the list of candidates.
